interest: This file provides valuable insight into the wartime legal status and administrative treatment of foreign-owned private and religious real property in imperial Japan during World War II. It highlights domestic American concerns—likely stemming from missionary societies, churches, or commercial stakeholders—regarding the security of pre-war investments and holdings following the outbreak of hostilities. Additionally, Secretary Hull's reply illustrates the State Department's understanding of Japanese property jurisprudence under the 1925 Alien Land Law and sheds light on how wartime belligerents maintained reciprocal mechanisms, such as enemy property custodians, without formally invalidating pre-war legal titles.
overview: This file comprises correspondence from late March 1944 between United States Senator Eugene D. Millikin of Colorado and Secretary of State Cordell Hull regarding the rights of American citizens and religious bodies to hold real property in Japan. Prompted by an inquiry from a Colorado constituent during World War II, Senator Millikin submitted questions asking whether Japan permitted private American citizens and religious institutions to own land prior to Pearl Harbor, and whether such ownership was permitted during the ongoing war. Secretary Hull replied that alien individuals, corporations, and religious institutions had been authorized to own land in Japan since 1925 (with properties of unincorporated missionary bodies held either by individual missionaries or Japanese juridical entities), and clarified that while wartime conditions barred enemy aliens from acquiring property and placed existing holdings under a Japanese authority analogous to the U.S. Alien Property Custodian, Japan was not believed to have invalidated pre-war American property titles.

subfiles.about: Senator Eugene D. Millikin transmits an inquiry from a Colorado constituent asking whether American citizens and religious institutions could own land in Japan before and during World War II.
subfiles.summary: Writing on Senate Committee on Finance stationery, Senator Eugene D. Millikin submits three specific inquiries to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on behalf of a constituent in Colorado. He asks whether the Japanese government permitted private American citizens to own land before Pearl Harbor, whether it permitted private American land ownership at present, and whether religious institutions were allowed to own property prior to the war. Millikin requests the State Department's authoritative views on these issues at an early convenience.
subfiles.title: Letter from Senator Eugene D. Millikin to Secretary of State Cordell Hull regarding land ownership in Japan

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Cordell Hull explains Japanese land ownership legislation since 1925 and the wartime administration of American-owned property in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull responds to Senator Millikin's inquiry, explaining that alien individuals, corporations, and religious institutions had been legally permitted to own land in Japan since 1925, with minor exceptions. He observes that because many American missionary societies were unincorporated, their properties were held either by individual missionaries or through juridical entities created under Japanese law. Hull further notes that while wartime information is limited, Japan is not believed to have invalidated pre-war American property titles, though such assets were placed under an official equivalent to the Alien Property Custodian and enemy aliens were precluded from acquiring land.
